Comprehensive two-stage technical pipeline with thoughtful design choices (entropy-based opacity regularization, pseudo-camera depth supervision, curriculum-based progressive refinement)
Extensive experimental validation including two major datasets, multiple strong baselines, and both quantitative metrics and user studies with detailed ablations
Practical efficiency enabling real-time navigation (11 FPS on RTX A6000)
Strong reproducibility with detailed implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, dataset information, and commitment to release code
Honest discussion of computational overhead and clear acknowledgment of limitations
Clear presentation with informative visualizations and well-structured paper organization

Evaluation limitations: distribution-based metrics may not fully capture 3D geometric accuracy; user study is small-scale video-based comparison; limited street-level quality assessment

Limited geographic and morphological diversity in evaluation - primarily US urban areas; unclear generalization to dense Asian cities, historic European towns, or other architectural traditions; fixed to 30 cm/pixel resolution
Incomplete analysis of geometric accuracy vs. appearance quality trade-off; potential for appearance hallucinations to violate physical constraints or introduce false details
Multi-date satellite imagery challenge acknowledged but not thoroughly addressed despite being critical for real-world deployment and temporal consistency

strengths: Addresses a practically motivated problem with clear applications in gaming, simulation, and urban visualization
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (DFC2019, GoogleEarth) with comparisons to 6+ baselines and thorough ablation studies (Tables 3-4)
Well-executed user study evaluating perceptual quality alongside quantitative metrics, demonstrating practical value
Clear and well-presented paper with effective visualizations and extensive supplementary materials
Good reproducibility practices including ethics statement, implementation details, and code release commitment
Reasonable qualitative results showing improvements in geometric accuracy and texture quality compared to baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (3DGS from Kerbl et al. 2023, standard appearance modeling, entropy-based opacity regularization, existing IDU framework) without substantial methodological innovation

Curriculum learning strategy lacks theoretical justification—the ad-hoc solution of cycling through elevation angles is effective but not properly analyzed; design choices for look-at point sampling (Section 3.2) are vaguely defined

Heavy and under-acknowledged reliance on pre-trained diffusion models (FlowEdit) and manual prompt engineering undermines claims of being 'open-domain'; sensitivity to prompt variations not studied, limiting generalization claims

Severely restricted evaluation scope: only urban scenes across limited geographic regions (NYC focus for GoogleEarth); no evaluation on rural, mountainous, or coastal areas; generalization to diverse architectural styles and geographies unknown

Incremental quantitative improvements: modest gains over baselines (e.g., Table 1 shows FID_CLIP of 30.13 vs. 26.69 for CoR-GS on DFC2019); improvements don't justify computational overhead; no statistical significance testing provided
Computational cost inadequately justified: 6-hour synthesis time on RTX A6000 for modest metric improvements; no runtime comparisons with baselines or analysis of cost-benefit trade-offs

Evaluation metric concerns: suitability of FID_CLIP and CMMD for assessing 3D geometric reconstruction from satellite data not validated; pixel-level metrics (SSIM, LPIPS) don't directly measure geometric accuracy critical for the application
Multi-date appearance variation (Figure 15) represents fundamental challenge acknowledged but not solved; diffusion-based refinement may mask rather than resolve temporal inconsistencies
Incomplete failure analysis: brief limitations section (page 9) lacks systematic discussion of failure modes, performance bounds, or scenarios where the method should not be used
Comparison fairness issues: different baselines evaluated on different subsets; CityDreamer and GaussianCity operate under different assumptions; baseline implementation details vary

Algorithm and mathematical clarity gaps: opacity regularization choice not justified; Figure 6(a) appears cherry-picked for the method's advantage (low elevation angles); Algorithm 1 underspecifies refinement details

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: generating immersive 3D urban scenes from readily available satellite imagery, with applications to gaming, robotics, and urban visualization
Well-motivated curriculum-learning strategy that progressively refines scenes from high to low elevation angles, grounded in empirical observations about 3DGS performance characteristics

Comprehensive experimental validation across two major datasets with multiple diverse urban environments and extensive comparisons to recent strong baselines (Sat-NeRF, EOGS, CityDreamer, GaussianCity, CoR-GS)
Consistent improvements across both distribution-based metrics (FID, CMMD) and pixel-level metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS), with user studies supporting geometric accuracy and perceptual quality gains
Elegant integration of existing components: clever combination of 3D Gaussian Splatting, appearance modeling, and pre-trained text-to-image diffusion refinement without domain-specific training
Strong reproducibility and transparency: detailed implementation details, clear dataset descriptions, evaluation protocols, promised code release, and LLM disclosure
Real-time rendering achieved (11 FPS on NVIDIA T4, 40 FPS on A100), enabling practical interactive applications

Thorough ablation studies (Tables 3-4) demonstrating the necessity and contribution of each component, including appearance modeling, opacity regularization, depth supervision, and curriculum learning
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: method primarily combines existing techniques (3DGS, appearance modeling, FlowEdit) rather than introducing new fundamental algorithms; main novelty is the curriculum-learning strategy and their integration
High computational cost (6 hours per scene on RTX A6000, 30,000 refinement iterations) with limited discussion of computational efficiency trade-offs and scalability to large metropolitan areas

Evaluation methodology limitations: ground truth is synthetic (GES renderings from trained 3D models) rather than measured 3D geometry; PSNR/SSIM against synthetic references cannot validate absolute geometric accuracy; user study limited in scope (qualitative, only DFC2019)

Insufficient analysis of satellite imagery limitations: building facades and street-level details are hallucinated by diffusion models due to inherent parallax constraints; limited exploration of failure modes and quality degradation in poorly-covered regions

Heavy dependence on pre-trained diffusion model (FlowEdit) quality; unclear sensitivity to prompt engineering; limited ablation on diffusion model choice; no analysis of when diffusion refinement creates plausible but geometrically incorrect structures

Multi-date appearance variation acknowledged but incompletely addressed: different dates introduce significant appearance changes (shown in Figure 15) that could compromise reconstruction quality and consistency

Scalability concerns: experiments limited to city block scale (~2km × 2km); unclear how artifacts compound in larger metropolitan areas or how method handles seamless transitions between adjacent regions

Limited societal impact discussion: while ethics statement provided, insufficient discussion of privacy/surveillance implications of generating high-fidelity 3D city models from satellite data, or guidance on appropriate use cases

strengths: Important and practical problem: Generating 3D urban scenes from satellite imagery addresses a valuable use case with readily available data at scale

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple datasets (DFC2019, GoogleEarth), user studies with 44 participants showing strong preference (≥82-90%), extensive quantitative comparisons against multiple baselines, and thorough ablation studies (Tables 3-4, Figure 9)

Impressive qualitative results: Significantly superior geometry and texture quality compared to state-of-the-art baselines, with effective handling of complex structures and reduced artifacts (Figure 7)
Well-designed hybrid approach: Two-stage pipeline effectively combines geometric grounding via 3D Gaussian Splatting with appearance synthesis via curriculum-based diffusion refinement
Real-time performance: Achieves 11 FPS on NVIDIA T4 and 40 FPS on MacBook Air M2, enabling interactive immersive exploration
Scalability demonstrated: Successfully reconstructs multi-block scenes (~1km × 512m) without boundary stitching artifacts, showing practical scalability to larger urban areas

Technical soundness: Components are well-justified (opacity regularization, pseudo-camera depth supervision, curriculum learning), with correct mathematical formulations and proper experimental design
Honest limitations discussion: Clear acknowledgment of constraints including fixed camera trajectories, reliance on nadir views, and potential artifacts in heavily occluded regions

Extensive implementation details: Comprehensive supplementary material with reproducibility information, including RPC error analysis (0.126 pixel maximum error), hyperparameter specifications, and memory profiling
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Individual components are largely adaptations of existing techniques (3DGS, FLUX diffusion, IDU from prior work); main contribution is systems integration and application rather than algorithmic innovation

Insufficient justification of design choices: Curriculum learning strategy's optimality lacks theoretical analysis; why specific configurations (N_p=2, N_p=6) outperform alternatives is not explored; text prompt sensitivity remains despite Table 10 analysis

Fundamental satellite imagery limitations inadequately addressed: Multi-date appearance variations (Figure 16) show drastic changes across different capture dates; RPC approximation errors (0.126 pixels) implications for final quality unclear; limited technical solutions provided for these core challenges

Evaluation scope limitations: Primarily aerial/drone perspectives with limited street-level evaluation; geographic scope concentrated in US cities; architectural diversity limited to modern urban areas without evaluation on informal settlements or historically unique environments

Quantitative metrics concerns: Heavy reliance on user studies without inter-rater reliability metrics; limited pixel-level quantitative validation for overlapping regions; per-scene results occasionally underperform (e.g., Mip-Splatting on scene 219) without explanation

Computational cost and accessibility: Requires 46GB GPU memory; 6.5 hours total (1h 35min reconstruction + 5h synthesis) per scene limiting practical deployment; FLUX model licensing/availability not discussed affecting reproducibility

Limited systematic failure mode analysis: While limitations mentioned, no systematic analysis of which urban structures cause degradation, how vegetation density affects results, or when transient object handling fails

Generalization questions: No evaluation on non-English regions or developing urban areas; limited evidence of robustness to extreme occlusion or non-rectilinear geometries; missing comparisons to domain-specific urban synthesis baselines (CityDreamer, GaussianCity)

Methodological clarity: Curriculum learning specifics unclear (what exactly constitutes 'uniformly placed points' in Section 3.2?); insufficient justification for why 2 diffusion samples per view is optimal (Figure 9c); diminishing returns analysis (Figure 22) raises questions about episode count selection

strengths: Addresses practical and well-motivated problem of generating detailed 3D urban scenes from satellite imagery alone without manual 3D annotations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including quantitative metrics on two datasets, user studies with 44 participants, and extensive ablation studies on both reconstruction and synthesis stages
Thorough supplementary material with implementation details, per-scene results, additional experiments on complex geometries, and extensive visualizations
Demonstrates system-level engineering with attention to practical constraints (RPC camera approximation, memory optimization, multi-block scalability, rendering efficiency at 11 FPS)
Shows ability to scale to large urban regions (~1km × 512m) with seamless handling of adjacent areas and complex structures (bridges, historical buildings)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (3D Gaussian Splatting, diffusion models, standard curriculum learning). Individual components are incremental - opacity regularization is standard entropy-based formulation, pseudo-depth supervision is straightforward, curriculum strategy lacks principled justification

Critical dependency on pre-trained diffusion models (FLUX.1): unclear how much improvement stems from the method versus the powerful generative model; no analysis of performance degradation with lower-quality diffusion models; potential for overfitting to model biases

Experimental evaluation concerns: (1) Metric selection flawed - acknowledges SSIM unreliability for generative tasks but uses it as primary metric; (2) No 3D geometric validation despite claiming to generate 3D scenes - missing comparison with ground truth 3D models or LiDAR data; (3) User study limited to 4 scenes with 44 participants; (4) Unfair baseline comparisons using different camera parameters (17° vs 45° elevation); (5) GoogleEarth evaluation uses rendered data rather than original satellite imagery

Technical soundness issues: (1) Pseudo-camera depth supervision using monocular depth estimation could propagate known biases - no ablation showing benefit versus geometry consistency alone; (2) Multiple diffusion samples (Ns=2) averaged without analysis of systematic averaging artifacts or sensitivity to Ns; (3) RPC camera approximation error acknowledged up to 0.864 pixels; (4) Curriculum learning rationale (why decreasing elevation angles) lacks principled analysis

Incomplete technical analysis: appearance modeling per-image embeddings not analyzed for generalization to novel views; no sensitivity analysis for satellite resolution, viewing angle variation, or seasonal changes; hyperparameter choices (λop, λdepth) appear dataset-specific with no principled selection criteria

Reproducibility and scalability challenges: requires ~6 hours training and 46GB peak memory on RTX A6000; method sensitive to specific pre-trained model versions; exact prompt engineering strategy not fully specified; high computational barriers limit accessibility; no indication of code release

Limited analysis of failure modes and generalization: acknowledged limitations on complex geometries and occluded regions but no systematic failure case analysis; no evaluation on diverse city types, climates, or architectural styles; method appears optimized for dense urban layouts

Method conceptual straightforwardness: IDU process (Algorithm 1) is iterative render-edit cycles - conceptually simple; curriculum is just progressive single parameter change; FlowEdit-based refinement is direct application of prior work; represents engineering solution rather than algorithmic innovation

strengths: Novel hybrid framework effectively combining 3D Gaussian Splatting with diffusion-based refinement for a well-motivated problem; satellite-specific optimizations (opacity regularization, pseudo-camera depth supervision, appearance modeling) are thoughtfully designed

Rigorous experimental validation with comprehensive comparisons against five recent baselines (Sat-NeRF, EOGS, CoR-GS, CityDreamer, GaussianCity) on two major datasets with extensive user studies (44 participants achieving 90-94% win rates)
Practical system achieving real-time performance (11 FPS model, 40 FPS consumer hardware) with demonstrated multi-block scalability and clear applications; eliminates need for costly 3D annotations

Thorough supplementary material with detailed implementation, resource analysis, sensitivity studies, and honest discussion of limitations; comprehensive ablation studies validate each component's necessity
Strong technical execution with well-designed loss functions, sound design choices (e.g., Pearson correlation for depth), and mathematically correct formulations throughout
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty; individual components are existing techniques (3DGS [33], standard appearance embeddings [35], FlowEdit [26], straightforward curriculum learning); contribution is primarily in integration and application rather than novel algorithms

Evaluation scope limited to primarily North American cities with relatively homogeneous architecture; only 4 additional AOIs for generalization testing; limited evaluation across diverse climate regions and non-Western urban styles; no explicit architectural style diversity analysis

Design choice justification incomplete: hyperparameters (λ_op=10, λ_depth=0.5) chosen through experimentation with limited theoretical grounding; opacity regularization entropy formulation not compared to alternatives; IDU hyperparameter tuning guidance unclear

Fixed heuristic camera trajectory acknowledged as potentially missing blind spots; multi-sample diffusion compromise (N_s=2) reduces visual diversity to minimize artifacts; coverage metric saturates around 0.75 suggesting potential fundamental limits

Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned, diffusion-based refinement adds subjective element, multi-stage training pipeline complexity, substantial computational requirements (~5.5 hours per scene), and diffusion sampling strategy introduces stochasticity

Limited failure analysis; no detailed breakdown of performance on specific challenging urban features (dense vegetation, water bodies, overpasses); transient object handling demonstrated but not systematically evaluated; Scene-219 exception not deeply investigated

Computational cost remains substantial despite efficiency claims (46 min reconstruction + 5 hours synthesis); real-time deployment (40 FPS) only after offline training; multi-block scalability (~9 hours) resource-intensive; not truly real-time for end-to-end synthesis

Evaluation metrics focused on appearance (FID/LPIPS) which may underestimate geometric distortions; geometric accuracy validated only on DFC2019 LiDAR; GoogleEarth validation relies on indirect GES renders; user study on geometric accuracy combined with perceptual quality without separate geometric assessment
